MANN, LOUIS CLAIBORNE, Son of Alsey and Mary Louis Claiborne Mann. 

Born in Haywood County, July 15, 1900.

Register of Deeds. Scotch-Irish descent. 

Single. Paternal grandparents, Richard and Harriot Taylor Mann. Maternal grandparents, William (Uncle Billie) and

County. Member of Methodist Episcopal Church and a Democrat. Elected Regis ter of Deeds in Aug., 1932, to succeed the late Thomas B. Claiborne, who died in office. Was again elected in Aug., 1934, each time by an outstanding majority.

HULL, CORDELL, Lawyer; statesman; born Overton Co. (now Pickett 

Co.) Tenn., Oct. 2, 1871; son of William and Elizabeth (Riley) Hull; father's occupation, farmer. Educated in schools of Ohio; and Cumberland University, Lebanon, Tenn., graduating from the latter June, 1891. In early life engaged in farming and lumber business. Member K. of P.; Democrat. Formerly a representative in the Lower House, Tenn. 

Legislature; former Judge of the 5th 

Judicial Circuit; former member of Congress from the 4th congressional District of Tenn.; soldier Co. H, 4th

Regiment Tenn. Vol. Infantry during 

Spanish-American War with rank of captain. Defeated for reelection to Congress in the Republican landslide of 1924, but was again elected to his former seat as Congressman from the 4th Congressional Dist. in the following election, serving until his election to the United 

States Senate in 1930. Served in the 

Senate until his appointment as Secretary of State in 1933, in the cabinet of 

President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Judge 

Hull during his services in the Congress of the U. S. attracted World-wide attention mainly through his knowledge of tariff and tax matters; is now regarded as perhaps the leading authority on these questions in the entire universe. 

Since he has become ranking member in the cabinet of the U. S., he has had occasion to deal with many problems affecting policies in various countries of the world; has proved his ability as a statesman on a thousand fields. Is prominently mentioned as the Democratic candidate for the presidency of the United States in 1940.

CHAPEL HILL HARGROVE, MRS. LOUSINA BELL, 

Hotel owner and Operator; born at 

Lillards Mill, Marshall County, June 26, 1860; descent, Scotch-Irish; daughter of 

William Euriah Cundiff, miller and 

Emily Jane (Clift) Cundiff; married 

John Alexander Hargrove February 18, 1883; paternal grandparents Jonathan 

B. and Sarah Ann (Trigg) Cundiff; maternal grandparents Isaac and Nancy (Malone) Rainey. Attended public schools of Marshall County; Lillie Hill 

Academy. Democrat; member of M. E. 

Church, South, W.C.T.U., P.T.A.; Pres. 

of local order of U.D.C.; Pres. Ladies' 

Missionary Society. Began her career as a teacher in the public schools of Marshall County, in which field she continued for 10 years; at the end of that time she was married, moved to Culleoka, where she lived for 8 years; returning to Marshall County, she lived at Lillards Mill for a number of years, where she and her husband were engaged in the milling business; then removed to Chapel Hill where with her husband she entered the mercantile business in 1916. Has been one of the most active women in her section in the business world as well as in social and civic activities. Regards the most outstanding achievement of her career that of securing the erection of the Nathan Bedford Forrest memorial at Chapel Hill, the place of his birth; this memorial was made possible by private subscription which she secured almost singlehandedly and by state appropriations made by the legislature of 1927; after this appropriation was made, she was commissioned by Governor Austin

Peay with full authority over the erection of this monument. Her father was a soldier in the Confederate Army during the Civil War, her uncle was also a Confederate soldier, serving as Captain under General Nathan Forrest. She is the mother of three children:-John 

Garnett, Mrs. Lou Emma Kerr, and William Evans; the latter was a soldier in the U. S. Army during the World War, serving with the A.E.F. in France for 

22 months.

His wife came from one of Tenn's most distinguished families.

U. of Chatt. Married G. Mance Sherrill, 

Dec. 30, 1922. She has one son, Wm. 

Marion Sherrill, born July 26, 1930. Her paternal grandparents were Nichalos P. 

and Irene Eldridge Frazier. Mr. Frazier fought in the Civil War under Nathan 

Bedford Forrest. Her maternal grand parents are William and Amanda Rowe 

Kelly. She is a member of M. E. Church

South, Women's Democratic Club and 

Eastern Star. She is a democrat and belongs to P.T.A.; served as Chief Deputy 

Circuit Court Clerk 3 years prior to her election as Circuit Court Clerk in Aug. 

1934, where she served 4 years. The first woman to hold this office in Hamilton County, and the first woman to hold any office after her husband has held it.

SHULL, DR. VIVION FREDERICK, 

Born at Peoria, Illinois, on May 8, 1901; 

German descent; son of John Howard 

Shull (electrician) and Rachel Givler

Shull. Paternal grandparents: Freder ick Augustus Shull and (Elsworth); maternal grandparents: Samuel Givler and

Frances Vandeventor Givler. Attended the public schools of Ill.; Fox-River 

Academy, Sheridan, Ill.; Emmanuel Missionary College, Garren Springs, Michigan; College of Medical Evangelist, Los 

Angeles, Cal.; M.D., 1930. Received diploma from D.N.B. same year; National board of medical examiners. Dr. Shull interned at the Nashville General Hospital for one year. He then practiced medicine at Grand Rapids, Michigan, for one year. He was then medical director at the Wabash Valley Sanitarium at La 

Fayette, Ind. from 1931-1933. In 1934 he came to Chatt. and entered the general practice of medicine. In April, 1936, he opened the Chatt. Hospital, a non-profit organization in conjunction with the Institute of Health and Healing, Inc., in order to foster and develop the Budget Help Plan, which is a co-operative medical group plan. The founders of this plan instituted it with the objective of bringing adequate medical care and hospitals within the reach of the great middle classes. This work in Chatt. has operated in conjunction with the projects of the 

Institute of Health and Healing and its rural estate, as described elsewhere.

(See page 

7.) He is the father of one child, Betty Gay, who was born June 6, 1933. Dr. Shull is one of Chattanooga's outstanding young physicians and surgeons.

THRASHER, WILKERS T., Born at 

Chatt., Tenn., on June 14, 1893; a Register of Deeds, Hamilton County; Scotch- 

Irish descent; married Louise McCahill on Sept. 6, 1920. Son of Jessie Scaife (lawyer and minister) and Lillie Wilkers 

Thrasher; paternal grandparents: John 

Thrasher and ( ); maternal grand parents: William Clay Wilkers and Phil adelphia Clay Wilkers. He attended public schools of Chatt.; Knoxville College of 

Law; Chatt., Tenn., LL.B., 1926. He is a member of the Presbyterian Church, Masons, Shrine, Eagles, and Elks American

Chatt. Her hobby is reading.

WILSON, HELEN LOUISE, Born in 

Oklahoma; a teacher of dancing; daugh ter of Dr. Samuel Warren and Jessica

Oscar Grogan, in Dec. Attended the public schools of Okla. and Calif.; Boswells School of New York City; graduate work, Dancing Masters of America. A 

member of the Tri-State of D.M. of A.;

the First Christian Church. Miss Wilson began her career as a dancer in musical comedies in New York, which work she pursued for a period of ten years, traveling throughout North America with both vaudeville and musicals. She was under contract with the Bohemians, Inc., of New

York City, and performed in such shows as the Greenwich Village Follies, No Other 

Girl, The Squawl, Dearest Enemy, and other Broadway shows. In 1933 Miss

Wilson moved to Chatt. where she opened a school of dancing, conducting her school at the famous Read House for a time, located on 8th St. where she is now located. She is one of the most outstanding teachers of dancing in her section of the state, having an average student enrollment of 175, consisting of all ages. 

Her father, Dr. Samuel Warren Wilson was a surgeon in the U.S. Army during the World War. He served with the 

A.E.F. with the famous Rainbow Divi sion, for a period of eighteen months.

Warner of Chatt.

CHURCH HILL HAMILTON, JOHN DAVID, Born at 

Church Hill, Tennessee on October 9, 1864, of Scotch-Irish parentage. His parents were John S. and Bettie Ott 

Hamilton; he married Mollie Kincheloe.

Mr. Hamilton has served in the Tennessee legislature for five terms 1923-25-27-31- 37. He has been a member of the county court of Hawkins County for almost a half-century. He was a member of the state board of education for a period of six years.

Each time he has served in the legislature he has made a creditable record and also each time he has been appointed to the most important committees in the House, serving as chairman twice of the House Finance Ways and Means Committee. His occupation, besides his political duties, is that of a farmer and stock trader. His paternal grandparents were John B. and ( > 

Hicks Hamilton; his maternal grandparents were David and ( ) ( ) Ott.

He was educated in the public schools of Hawkins County and at Carson- 

Newman College. Member of the Baptist 

Church, Democrat, Mason. His father served in the Civil War for four years. 

He has always been an active leader in church and civic affairs. He is Hawkins 

County's most outstanding citizen. He is the father of four children. His hobby is rural education. 

CLARKSVILLE BROADBENT, A. B., Statesman; born on a farm in Kentucky of English parentage November 21, 1885. He moved to Tennessee when a boy, locating at 

Clarksville, where he now lives; after completing his common school education he attended law school, completing this course in 1912; passed the State Bar examination and began the practice of law at Clarksville, remaining there throughout the years that followed; acquired an enviable practice in his profession; has been for many years chair man of the State Board of Law Exam iners for Tennessee. In 1922, 1924, and 1926 he managed the successful campaigns for governor of the late 

Hon. Austin Peay; elected to the State

Senate from the 15th Senatorial Dist. of 

Tennessee in 1930, for the session of the 

65th General Assembly; elevated to the speakership of that body; re-elected to the senate in 1932; managed the successful campaign of the Hon. Gordon Browning for governor in 1936; elected 

Secretary of State, January 13th, 1937 without opposition. Is the son of P. H. and Katherine (Jones) Broadbent; has never married.

1911, teaching in a one-room log schoolhouse in Carter Co.; he continued in this profession for a period of twelve years through all the grades and high school work, serving for eight years as principal of Carter Co. High Schools. In 1923 he was elected to the office of Co. Supt. of 

Schools of Carter Co., by the Co. Court; was re-elected by that body until 1936, at which time he was elected by popular vote. Since the beginning of his services as Supt. there have been more buildings constructed than ever before in all the history of the country which buildings are mainly brick and stone. In 1928 he was elected Pres. of the East Tenn. County 

Supt. Conference, serving until 1930, at which he was elected Pres. of the East 

Tenn. Education Association at Knox ville, an organization consisting of over five thousand teachers. He was admitted to the bar in 1930, and at the termination of his present official services for the county will be engaged in the practice of law. His grandfather, John Moore, was a soldier in the Civil War on the side of the Union, serving in the 13th Tenn. Reg. 

He is the father of six children: Mrs. 

Marie Street, Byron, Vaughn, Robert, Billie, and Nelle.

MORELAND, JOHN MILARD, Sheriff and Farmer. Of Irish-Dutch descent. 

Born in Carter Co., Tenn., Sept. 7, 1892.

He is the son of Elbert Moreland and 

Katherine (Grindstaff) Moreland; paternal grandparents, John Moreland and ); maternal grandparents, Jacob Grindstaff and Chrissice Reece. Attended schools of Carter Co., and is a member of Free Will Baptist Church; 

Republican; Jr. O.U.A.M.; Chamber of

Commerce. Married Bertha Lipps. He began his life as a farm hand after going from Tennessee to Kansas at fourteen years, inheriting a desire to travel from his father who had at the time of his death been in every state in the Union. 

After spending four years in Kansas, he went to California for two years and then returned to Tennessee where he became engaged with a lumber co. In 1926 he was first elected sheriff of Carter Co. and re-elected in 1928, then was elected again in 1932 and re-elected twice since, serving in all for a period of ten years.

He has made a reputation as a peace officer, which will long be remembered by the people he served. He also installed the first police radio for Carter Co., which he financed and was later assumed by the county. He is the father of four children: Myrtie, Robert, G. L., and Bertie (deceased).

He is the second to succeed himself during the past twenty years and his services as sheriff have been outstanding for his strict enforcement of all laws especially the enforcement of the liquor law; during his first term of office he confiscated more than two hundred moonshine stills in Unicoi Co. Prior to his election as sheriff he served as a member of the Unicoi Co. Court from 

1930 until his election as sheriff. From 

1918 until 1930 he was engaged in the mercantile business at Unicoi from which district he was elected to county court. 

He was also engaged as a railway brakeman for a period of about five years; for four years from 1930-34 he was chairman of the Unicoi Office Republican 

Executive Committee. His grandfather

Timberlake was a soldier in the Civil War, fighting on the side of the Confederacy. He is a distant cousin of the famous Taylors of the Happy Valley section of Carter Co., both former governors of Tenn. He is the father of two children, Robert N. and Joe Galloway, both students in high school.

COWLEY, JOHN POLK, JR., Merchant and farmer. Scotch-Irish-English descent, born at Kelso, Tenn., Feb. 23, 1880, son of John Polk Cowley, farmer, banker, stock dealer, and Sarah Locker; paternal grandparents, Ben Cowley and Margaret

Lincoln Co. Quarterly Court serving for a longer period than any other man in his county.

PIERCE, PROF. JOEL N., Supt. of 

Schools of Greene Co. Born at Moshein, Greene Co., Jan. 7, 1878. Son of John E. 

Pierce and Sarah Kenney Pierce; father's occupation, farmer. Paternal grandparents, James Pierce and Mary Green; maternal grandparents, Harmon Kenney and Nancy Price; attended public schools of Greene Co.; Oakland Seminary, A.B., 1899; University of Tenn., 1906; East

Tenn. State Teachers College, 1912; and is a member of Methodist Episcopal Church; Republican; 1.0.0.F.; Jr. 

O.U.A.M.; Rotary; East Tenn. Teachers 

Assn.; State School Officers Assn.; State

Teachers Association. Married Miss Deb bie Jones on July 11, 1900. Prof. Pierce began his career as a teacher in the public schools of Greene Co., continuing in this profession for a period of fifteen years. 

He was elected Supt. of Schools of Greene Co. in 1913, serving until 

1927, being elected seven times without opposition by the County Court of Greene

Co.; he declined re-election to become engaged in the real estate business in which he was engaged for a period of eight years at Greeneville. He was again elected Supt. of Schools of Greene Co. in 1935 by the Greene Co. Court and in 

1936 was re-elected by popular vote without opposition. Prof. Pierce is regarded as one of the leading educators of his section of the state and his long tenure of office is evidence of both his efficiency and popularity with the people of his county. Through his untiring efforts as administrator of the school system of 

Greene Co., many improvements have been brought about-at the beginning of his services there was not a high school in the county-transportation, consolidation and many other improvements have been made until today the county ranks among the very first in the state. In 1917 Prof. Pierce became president of the East Tenn. Educational 

Assn.

In 1920 he was elected president 

Public School Officers Assn. for the state, and in 1925 he was appointed by Hon. 

Austin Peay, then governor, as the East

Tenn. member of State Text-book Com mission of Tenn. He is the father of two children, Mrs. Kate Jeffers and a son, Paul Jones, Atty., who died on 

Oct. 18, 1931; he has four grandchildren: 

Paul, Helen, Louise, and Phil Jeffers. 

RUSH, JAMES A., Auctioneer, Real 

Estate operator, farmer, livestock dealer. 

Born near Greeneville, Tenn., July 31, 1873; Scotch-Irish descent. Son of John 

M. Rush and Alice Campbell Rush. Father's occupation, farmer, trader, and shipper. Paternal grandparents, Capt. 

David Rush and Martha Smith; maternal grandparents, Adam Peck Campbell and ); attended public schools of

O.U.A.M.; D. of A. Married Miss Ora 

White on Nov. 25, 1903. She died on 

Jan. 13, 1938. Mr. Rush in his early life was a teacher in the public schools of Greene County where he served for a period of five years. After the expiration of this period he became an auctioneer, in which he has been engaged for the past forty-five years, conducting sales in many other states, consisting of real estate and livestock. In this line of work he is one of the most outstanding in the entire state. For a number of years he has been engaged in the real estate business, having been one of the largest operators in his section of the state. He is also one of the leading livestock dealers in his county, handling all kinds of livestock. He was a member of the 67th General Assembly of Tenn. 

as a direct representative from Greene

Co. He was assigned to most of the

STYKE, QUINCY N., Sheriff of Greene 

Co. Born in Jefferson, Ashe Co., N.

Carolina, April 9, 1885. Of Scotch-Irish- 

Dutch descent; son of William M. Styke and Amanda E. Sapp Styke. Father's occupation, farmer. Paternal grandparents, Rev. J. W. Styke and Tamsey 

Eller; maternal grandparents, David 

Sapp and Zilpha Reedy. He attended public schools of N. Carolina; Smith Co., Va., High School, 1902; and is a member of Methodist Episcopal Church So.; 

Democrat. Married Miss Winnie Ander son, Smith County, Va., on Jan. 20, 1908.

Mr. Styke was first elected Sheriff of 

Greene Co. in Aug., 1932, by an overwhelming majority, and he was again elected to the office of Sheriff of Greene 

Co. in Aug., 1936, which office he now holds. Prior to his election as Sheriff he served for four years as Deputy Sheriff of Coake Co. under Flint Ray, then 

Sheriff of that County, and as Deputy 

Sheriff of Greene Co. for two years under 

Sheriff J. A. Noel. He has been for the past ten years a member of the 

Greene Co. Board of Education. During his many years of public service as an officer, he has had an opportunity to become acquainted with the affairs of this County and has served in the capacity as a peace officer commendable in many respects. Prior to his entering public life he was engaged in farming and livestock raising in which pursuit he is still engaged. Both of his grandfathers were soldiers in the Confederate army during the Civil War. His grandfather Styke was a Captain and was wounded in the Battle of Chickamauga. 

He is the father of four children: Mrs. 

Selma Wisecarver; Georgia Eunice, teacher; Q. N., Jr.; and Mrs. Ruth S. 

Laughters, who died on Feb. 24, 1936. 

His hobby is livestock trading.

SUSONG, EDITH O'KEEFE, Pub lisher of Greeneville Daily Sun. Born in 

Greeneville, Tenn.; Scotch-Irish descent. 

Daughter of William Henry O'Keefe, deceased, and Quincy Marshall O'Keefe. 

Paternal grandparents, Thomas Cornelius 

O'Keefe and Sarah Ingles O'Keefe; maternal grandparents, John Coleman Mar shall and Martha Arnold Marshall. 

She attended Miss Ellett's School, Richmond, Va.; Agnes Scott College, Atlanta, Ga.; and is a member of Andrew Johnson

Woman's Club; Nolichucky Chapter 

D.A.R.; Business and Professional Women's Club; Hugenot Society; Tenn. Press and Authors' Club. Married David 

Shields Susong on Sept. 26, 1911. She is the mother of two children: Alex 

Elbert of Washington, D. C., and Martha 

Arnold of Greeneville. In 1916, she took over the Weekly Democrat, which was established in 1879, and in 1920 bought the Daily Sun, combining the two papers. 

She was the first woman to serve as director of the Southern Newspaper Publishers' Association and the first woman to serve as director of the Greene County 

Chamber of Commerce, holding that position for years. She served as president of the Tenn. Federation of Women's 

Clubs, 1927-28, and 1928-29; was president of the Tenn. Woman's Press and 

Author's Club; director of Tenn. Business and Professional Women's Club; 

secretary of Greene County Library As sociation and other local offices, including president of Andrew Johnson Club. She was a member of the Tenn. NRA Board, and one of the five members appointed by Governor Hill McAlister on the Tenn. 

Educational Commission. She was a member of the State Textbook Committee which selected the books for the schools of Tenn. in 1936. For the past several years Mrs. Susong has been one of East Tennessee's most colorful figures.

She has been engaged in the promotion of many public and civic improvements and her services as a public speaker have been in constant demand over the entire state and in many other states. 

In her many connections she has proven her ability and her fidelity to duty.

HALLS BROWNING, MRS. BERTHA, Teacher. 

Born in Milau, Tenn., Sept. 2, 1882.

Daughter of William Clayton Carr and 

Mary Florence Martin Carr; father's occupation, merchant and farmer. Paternal grandparents, Thomas Carr and Mary 

Tatum; maternal grandparents, Lemuel 

Martin and Nancy Sheppard. Attended public schools of Weakley Co.; Henderson High, 1897; Georgie Roberson College, Henderson, Tenn., B.S., 1901; Union 

University, Jackson, Tenn., A.B., 1924;

Graduate Work at Union University. 

She is a member of Church of Christ;

Democrat. Married Edmond Marvin 

Browning on April 26, 1910. Mrs. Browning began her teaching career as a teacher in the public schools of Weakley County at Milau in 1901. In 1903 she moved to 

Lauderdale County to continue in her chosen profession, teaching first at Edith then at Curve, serving as principal at both places. She was then employed in 

Gibson County for a period of two years, being the first lady principal at the 

Gibson High School. She moved again to Lauderdale County in 1910 after her marriage and resumed her teaching in 1911, at which time she was made principal of the Nankipoo High School, which post she has held ever since. She was a teacher of Education and History at 

Union University at Jackson, Tenn., for three summers, and has been a coach of basketball for the past fifteen years, having produced some of the leading teams in West Tenn. Mrs. Browning is one of the most widely known lady educators in her section of the state, having been actively engaged in the profession for a period of thirty-six years. She has been actively engaged in all church and civic work for many years, having taught a class in Sunday school for a number of years, and has been instrumental in many civic and public improvements during the past several years. She is the mother of one very talented daughter, Mrs. Edna 

Browning McBride, teacher of mathematics at David Libscomb College, Nashville, Tenn. Her hobby is flower gardening.

HARTSVILLE HAMMOCK, MISS MAYNE, Banker, 

Mayor of Hartsville, Tenn. Born in 

Hartsville, Tenn., Feb. 28, 1888; Scotch- 

Irish descent; daughter of Wm. M. Hammock and Betsy M. Allan; father's occupation, Atty., ex-Judge. Paternal grandparents, Lemuel Hammock and ); maternal grandparents, Arch 

Allan and Frances Day. Attended public schools of Trousdale Co.; Ward-Belmont,

B. S., 1907. She is a member of Baptist 

Church; Democrat; Association of Bank 

Women; Civic Club. Miss Hammock has been actively engaged in the banking business for twenty-six years, having risen from the place of a bookkeeper to the management of the Bank of Hartsville, established in 1884, and one of the largest country banks in the state and also one of the fastest-growing banks in the state. Miss Hammock was elected 

Mayor of Hartsville in 1936, and she is the only woman mayor in the state of Tennessee, having been elected over formidable opposition by a large majority. 

She is Treasurer of the local Red Cross, a place she has held since its organization in Trousdale County. For the last thirty years she has been active in the affairs of the Baptist Church at Hartsville, Tenn.

She is one of the state's outstanding women, taking an active interest in all things which tend to better her community. Miss Hammock is the daughter of the late Wilson M. Hammock who for many years was Circuit Judge of ( ).

HUNTSVILLE BYRD, ROSCOE, Trustee; born in 

Scott County, Feb. 28, 1893; English descent; son of Geo. W. Byrd, public official and farmer, and Nancy Phillips; paternal grandparents: Oliver P. Byrd and Han nah Sharp; maternal grandparents: Jeremiah Phillips and Malinda Delk; attended public schools of Scott Co.;

Draughons Business College, Knoxville, 

Tenn.; and is a member of Baptist 

Church; Mason; J.O.U.A.M.; Republican. 

Married May Owens, Aug. 17, 1922. Mr.

Byrd was first elected Trustee in 1922 and has served continuously since that time; he is now serving his 8th term; he has at times had overwhelming majorities and at others not so large but has had opposition each time. His tenure of office constitutes a record for the county both as to continuous terms and as to the number of years serving; the condition of his books attest his efficiency as a public official. He enlisted May 17, 1917 in the U.S. Army for service in the 

World War; he served overseas for about ten months participating in the operations on the Champagne front being severely wounded. He returned to the 

States landing at Newport News, Jan. 

1919, and was discharged May, 1919. His grandfather was a member of the Home 

Guard during the Civil War. Mr. Byrd's father, Geo. W. Byrd, preceded him as

Trustee of Scott Co. and has served six years as such, father and son having served continuously since 1916. His hobbies are hunting and baseball.

MEDEARIS, WILLIAM DAVIS, 

Evangelist; born at Tullahoma, Tenn., Nov. 10, 1913; Scotch-Irish; single; son of Frank Lipscomb and Mary Gladys 

Wheatley Medearis; paternal grandparents are Washington Davis and Lucy 

Allen Medearis; maternal grandparents are William Harris Wheatley and Olivia 

V. Willis. Attended the public schools of Dallas, Texas and Marshall County, Tenn.; Hume-Fogg High, 1934; Harding 

College, Searcy, Ark., B.A. degree. A member of the Church of Christ; a Democrat. Mr. Medearis is still pursuing his education, taking up his studies in L.S.U. after which he is to enter Harvard and will then travel abroad. Notwithstanding his age he is recognized as one of the most proficient Bible scholars of any other within many years of his age; his knowledge of divine history is recognized by all who know him. During all of his school life he made a progress unsurpassed and in all school activities he was sought after as a leader. Like "The 

War of the Roses, "" a political battle of the late nineties in Tenn., he and his brother in their senior high school year were chosen by their respective factions of the student body and were candidates for the honor of Student Council each receiving more than nine hundred votes which honor he won over his brother by seventy-five votes. He continued to receive school honors and while at Harding 

College he won the Founders Medal of that school. From his early childhood he has taken an active part in all religious affairs, yielding to early parental training. He began the study of the 

Bible at an early age being able to quote a large portion of the Bible at the age of eleven; when only eighteen years of age he was a teacher in the regular Sunday School in one of the largest churches in 

Nashville. He comes of one of the oldest pioneer families of Middle Tenn., many of his ancestors participating in many of the military conflicts. His greatgrandfather Medearis served as Capt. in the Confederate Army during the Civil 

War.

FLY, DR. JAMES CLAGETT, Physi cian and surgeon; born in Hickman 

County on June 16, 1883; Irish descent; son of James Madison Fly (farmer) and

Caroline Primm Fly. Paternal grandparents: George Washington Fly and 

Winifred Ann Elizabeth Lacy; maternal grandparents: John T. Primm and Ce cilia C. Gant Primm. Attended the public schools in Hickman County, Tenn.; high school in Louisiana; Vanderbilt

University, 1912-16; Public Health 

Course, Vanderbilt, 1931; member of the 

M. E. Church So.; Mason. Dr. Fly has resided in Kingston, Tenn. since 1920 

serving as full time County Health Of ficer for the entire time. Prior to this he practiced medicine at Carthage, Tenn. for a period of about a year and spent over two years with the Medical Corps of the U. S. Army. Enlisting in June 

1917 he served as a first lieutenant for approximately one year and as captain until his discharge at Camp Taylor the latter part of 1919. He spent about 14 months of his service overseas. His service overseas was varied; serving in various hospitals, he was transferred to the army of occupation and was stationed at Ruxenbourg, Germany, from which point he later returned to the 

U. S. via Brest, France landing at Camp 

Mills, N. Y. and thence to Camp Taylor by way of Atlanta, Ga. Dr. Fly's wide experience has especially fitted him for a life of service to humanity in his chosen calling of improving the public health. During his service as County 

Health Officer of Roane County such com municable diseases as typhoid and smallpox have been practically eliminated as menaces to public health. Cases of diphtheria have been greatly lessened and tuberculosis has been reduced approximately 50 per cent. 

His hobbies are hunting and fishing.

KINSER, JOHN MALCOLM, Drug gist; born in McMinn County on Nov.

Macon, Ga. He is a member of the

Legion; Democrat. Mr. Kinser is in the drug business in Kingston, where he has been located for four years. Prior to this Mr. Kinser had travelled for a wholesale drug concern in the Southwest, worked for his father in the drug business, and was in the drug business for himself in Etowah, Tenn. Mr. Kinser voluntarily enlisted in the army for service in the World War in Sept. 1918, was sent to University of Tenn. officers' training camp and was discharged on 

Dec. 7, 1918, following the signing of the Armistice in November. He has established a reputation as a dependable druggist and as a business man interested in all activities tending toward the improvement of his community. He is the father of two children: Martha Laura, 14, and Alfred Thomas, 12. Mr. Kinser is a direct descendant of Archibald Roane, one of the early governors of Tenn. and the man for whom Roane 

County is named. His great-great-grandfather Thomas Cantrell, due to a joining of the family lines, was also his greatgreat-great-grandfather. This ancestor was a soldier in the Revolutionary War, and is buried in McMinn County, Tenn. 

His great-great-great-grandfather, Robert Cooke, was an officer under George 

Washington in the Revolutionary War. 

Mr.

Kinser's hobbies are fishing and hunting.

HICKS, WM. GLENN AND ED. L., Sons of Sidney P. Burton and Marcellous

At- tended public schools of Knox County; 

the U. of T. Ed. L. Hicks and Wm. Glenn 

Hicks are owners of the Post Sign Co., Inc. the largest of its kind in the South as well as being the most modern and doing business all over the U.S. as well as foreign countries. The owners are brothers, the former is President and the latter is Vice-President of the company. In 1910 Ed. L. Hicks, a young man not long out of school, went to work for Mr. Post and in 1914 he bought half the business and became a partner in what was known as the Post Sign Co. Hicks bought his one-half interest. The company has passed its half-century mark being the oldest in the South. Their grandfather Hicks was a captain in the

Civil War. Both have been President of the Shrine Club (Kerbela Temple).

Culture; born at Jellico, Tenn., Jan. 25, 1894; English descent; daughter of Cal vin Lafayette Mundie (contractor) and 

Malinda Savannah Lynn Mundie; married William Lawson on Dec. 30, 1932; grandparents: paternal, William Mundie and ( ); maternal, Elijah Lynn and 

Emili Branham. Attended Kingston 

High, Kingston, Tenn. A member of the 

Broadway Baptist Church; Democrat.

Mrs. Lawson in her early career was engaged in newspaper work, traveling in special circulation work which she continued for a period of fifteen years. She then began the study of Beauty Culture, in which work she was engaged for several years. 

She received her training under the able instruction of Miss Carry 

Walter of New York and Paris; she then began the teaching of the Marinello System in Knoxville in which work she is now engaged; her school is located at 

4222 So. Gay St.; under her instruction many capable instructors and operators are stationed in many sections of East Tenn. She is recognized as one of the most capable and outstanding Beauty

Culture instructors in the entire country and her many charms, with her talents, make her one of the most popular women in Knoxville. Her grandfather Lynn was a soldier in the Confederate Army during the Civil War, serving for the entire duration of the conflict.

STOCKSBURY, WILLIAM H., Born at Rule, Union County, Tenn., on July 4, 1866; educator; married Ella Patterson

Jamison on Aug. 26, 1903; son of Alvis and Elizabeth Duke Stocksbury; grandparents: paternal, Jacob Stocksbury and

to date. During this time he has paid off a large indebtedness. Dr. Stocksbury is reputed to be an unusually fine instructor and good school manager. His reputation as a successful school manager is evidenced by the fact that he took over a number of schools that were down and out and built them up to a strong enrollment and high standing. He is an exceptionally fine disciplinarian and is considered one of the best school financiers. Dr. Stocksbury has had the opportunity to know and to deal best with practically all school problems that usually occur with the management of schools. He has taught from every grade in the public schools to the highest grades in colleges and universities. He is peculiarly adapted to make plain to his pupils the subjects he teaches. His illustrations are always lucid and to the point. The Knoxville Business College at present is enjoying the largest prosperity it has had since 1923. He is a 

Republican.

They settled in N. C., later going to 

Middle Tenn., where they have been among the leading families of the state for the past several generations. His people now live on the old homestead which was acquired by Federal grant about the year 1800.

Dur ing the Civil War he was three times placed before the firing squad because of his refusal to take the oath of allegiance to the Union. Because he had a son in the Confederate Army, he was in staunch sympathy with the Confederate cause.

FAULKNER, WALTER SANDERS, 

Lawyer; born Lebanon, Tenn., Nov. 23, 1874; English-Scotch descent; son of 

James Jones and Nora (Sanders) Faulkner; educated at Cumberland University, Lebanon, Tenn., and graduated from same with degree LL.D. in 1893; member of I.0.0.F., K.P.; Democrat; presidential elector Fourth District, Tenn., 1900; district attorney-general 8th Circuit of Tenn.; member of Christian church. General Faulkner was Dist. At torney-General of the eighth circuit of 

Tenn.; also served one term in State Sen ate, Chairman of the Investigating Com mittee, a committee vested with more power than any committee ever constituted in Tenn. He is the only man who ever served in the Tenn. legislature who, on completion of his service, gave his first salary to Tenn. charity. Gen. Faulkner is engaged in the general practice of law at Lebanon and enjoys practice in 10 or 11 surrounding counties. He is the author of several important and popular books. His latest work A Child's History and Interpretation of the Constitution, has received high commendation from learned lawyers, including the members of the 

State Appellate Courts and the Supreme 

Court of the U. S. He is the publisher of the Lebanon Banner. He has written editorials for this periodical which were widely reproduced and received many favorable comments. He is also presidential elector and a delegate to the Phil adelphia presidential convention.

TON, Teacher; born at Rutherford

Zumbro is one of the best qualified school men in the state and has for many years been a recognized leader in the educational activities of the state. Teachers; also a member of S.A.S.S. 

His school for many years has been a leading contender in all athletics. Professor Zumbro was a member of the committee which formed the present Constitution of the State Teachers Assn. of 

Tenn. He has been very active in all church, civic, and public affairs as well as educational work which results in many ways prove his worth to his community. He is the father of one son, John Stephens, a student in high school. 

His hobby is gardening.

Marcus Lafayette Mourfield and Mar garet Yost, on June 3, 1909; son of Nathaniel P. and Sophia Wilson; paternal grandparents: Drewry A. and Caroline 

Ballard Bacon; maternal grandparents:

John and Malinda Marney Wilson. 

tended the public schools of Loudon

Cherokee Country Club; Holston Country 

Club; Presbyterian Church (Cumberland) and a staunch Democrat. He has given his best service to all of these social, civil, and political fields. The main business interest with which Col. Bacon is connected is that of the manufacturing of hosiery and yarns; he operates large mills in Lenoir City and Loudon which business he began in 1906 as Secy. and 

Treasurer of the Loudon Hosiery Mills of Loudon; he became President and

General Manager in 1918 of this company

151 which was absorbed by the Charles H. 

Bacon Company in 1924. Col. Bacon has served on the staffs of three governors of Tennessee: first, Gov. Albert H. Rob erts in 1918; second, Austin Peay in 

1923; third, Henry H. Horton in 1928.

He has been a strong supporter of the Democratic party and its principles rendering a valuable service to the organization in every campaign during the last quarter of a century. He served for four years as a member of the State Executive

Committee of his party and as a member of the Quarterly County Court of Loudon 

County for two terms, receiving an unprecedented vote in each election for a candidate with or without opposition in his district. His service to the people of his county as a member of the Court merits the praise of his constituents and the respect of his colleagues. He is one of the most widely known businessmen in his section of the State-many in minor circles seek his wise and safe counsel. He is a recognized leader in many lines of endeavor in the State. 

His hobby is sports of all kinds. 

BREAZEALE, JEFFERSON IN- GRAM, Born in Loudon County, Tenn. 

on Aug. 2, 1875; Trustee of Loudon 

County; German descent; married Mary 

Bell Hill on May 29, 1897 who died May 

5, 1913; married Hannah Price on Nov. 

21, 1917; son of John G. and Mary Jane 

Blackburn Breazeale; father's occupation: farmer; paternal grandparents: 

James and Peggy Miller Breazeale. Attended the public schools of Loudon 

County; Loudon High, 1895; Achme High in Roane County; a member of Baptist

Eastern Star; D. of A.; Lions Club. Mr. 

Breazeale was first elected Trustee of 

Loudon County in Aug. 1932, re-elected in Aug. 1936; in his first two races he was without opposition; the third time he won by an overwhelming majority. Prior to his election as trustee he was Chair man of the County Board of Education serving in this capacity for a period of about eight years. In his early life he was engaged in the teaching professionteaching in the public schools of Loudon 

County for approximately twelve years, during which time and after which he was engaged in farming and livestock raising on the same farm lands which he still owns and operates. His wide experience and training have made him one of the county's best qualified men and his popularity is attested by the fact of his being three times elected to the office of Trustee. He is the father of nine children-seven by his first marriage: Lois, teacher at Knoxville; Stonewall Jackson, Supt. of Brase Foundry of 

Lenoir City; William Harrison, farmer;

Lou, Principal of Browder School; Nina, teacher in Staub School, Knoxville;

Lexie and Earl, both deceased. He has two others by his second marriage: Jefferson Ingram, Jr. and Mary Fay. His father was a soldier in the Civil War, fighting on the side of the Union for the entire duration of the conflict. His hobby is the support of education.

KOLLOCK, KYLE ANDERSON, Asst. 

Cashier of First National Bank; Insur ance, Real Estate; born in Loudon, Tenn. on Nov. 1, 1908; Scotch-Irish descent; married Sarah Denton on Jan. 10, 1937; son of Joseph H. and Beula H. Anderson; father's occupation: insurance and real estate; paternal grandparents: Joseph

Republican; Lions Club; Phi Kappa Al pha. Mr. Kollock was elected Asst.

Cashier of the First National Bank of

Mr. Kollock is the owner and operator of two farms in Loudon County, specializing in the raising of purebred Angus Cattle.

Kollock served with the rank of 1st Lt. in Inf. His grandmother Kollock distinguished herself during the Civil War for her bravery and consecration to the cause of the Union by delivering mail to the Union soldiers through the lines of the Confederate Army. His hobby is sports. Mr.

MCLEAN, MRS. MARYILYN EVE- LYN, Born at Sweetwater, Tenn. on April 

29, 1909; Beauty Parlor owner and operator; Irish-German-Dutch descent; daughter of Rev. S. G. and Rosa Frances 

Carden Grubb; paternal grandparents: 

Ulysses S. Grant and Martha Ann Taver 

Grubb; maternal grandparents: Wm.

Carden and Lorina Bell Glover Carden. 

Attended the public schools of Sweetwater, and Sweetwater High School; 

member of the First Baptist Church; Re publican; D. of A. Mrs. McLean began her business career in Knoxville, Tenn. in Oct. 1929; after a period of five years she moved to North Carolina where she remained for about two years; then she returned to Knoxville for a short time; she then moved to Loudon, where she is operating one of the most popular shops in her section of the State drawing trade from a large area. Mrs. McLean is one of the most popular women in her county taking an active part in all social and civic affairs which are for the betterment of conditions in her town and county. 

She is the mother of one talented daughter: Dorthy Geraldine, aged 10. Mrs. 

McLean is one of eleven children being one of the youngest whose father has served in the Baptist Ministry for more than two score years having been stationed in many places in East Tennessee. 

Her grandfather was a soldier in the

Civil War fighting on the side of the Union for the entire duration of the conflict. She has been interested for many years in short story writing; although not claiming to be an author she has written several stories which have appeared in some of the leading magazines—this she claims as a hobby.

LIVELY, WILLIAM SPENCER, Pub lic official; president Southern School of 

Photography; son of Joseph P. Lively; father's occupation, cabinet maker and undertaker; in early life he was a photographer; married Lela Jones, Dec. 10, 1878; Democrat; former city recorder; at present mayor of the city of McMinnville, Tenn.; member of Christian church; interested in furniture business. He is one of the nation's outstanding photographers. He has been employed by the 

U. S. Government to teach army students the art of photography. For many years he ran the Southern School of Photography at McMinnville and numbered among his former students are leading photographers the world over. At the

Chicago World Fair one of his pictures won first prize for being the largest photograph ever taken. The honors, prizes and awards which he has won are too numerous to mention, suffice to say he has won every honor worth mentioning in the field of photography.

MONROE, WILLIAM PRESTON, 

Judge; born in Union County, Tenn. on 

Nov. 20, 1886; Scotch-Irish; married

Callie Isabella Edmondson on July 14, 

1906; son of Horace Maynard and Luzana 

Elizabeth Graves Monroe; paternal grandparents: William George Monroe and 

Branson Monroe; maternal grandparents: Richard Graves and 

Elithia Fraker Graves. Attended the public schools of Union County; Hills 

Academy; Cumberland University, LL.B., 1911; a member of the Baptist (Missionary) Church; a Republican; Mason; 

Junior I.O.O.F.; Odd Fellows. Judge Monroe was elected as circuit judge of the second judicial circuit of Tenn. Aug. 3, 1934 for a term of 8 years. Prior to his election he was engaged in the general practice of law at Maynardville with practice in several adjoining counties. 

In the year 1918 he was elected to the 

State Senate from the 3rd Senatorial 

District and re-elected in 20-24-26-30-32. 

On each occasion he was appointed to the most important committees of the Senate.

He devotes a great deal of his time to church and civic affairs. He also has large real estate holdings. He is the author of Tennessee's Parole Law, which law was characterized by the American 

Bar Assn. as the greatest improvement in modern criminal jurisprudence to take place in the last century; he was also the co-author of the Tennessee State Highway Act. It is rare that a case upon which he has acted is reversed. He is the father of four children: Dr. Harmon 

Lawrence Monroe, Walter Preston Monroe, Irby Horace Monroe, Jessie Annie 

Lou Monroe. At the age of 16, Mr. Monroe was janitor of the same courthouse at Maynardville in which he now presides as circuit and chancery judge.

1918, term expiring while in France.

Completing the special course for Reserve 

Officers at the School of Fire, Ft. Sill, 

Okla.; Staff & Command School, Ft.

Field Art. Brigade.

BOYLE, VIRGINIA FRAZER, “Lead ing literary woman of the nation." She was born near Chattanooga, ( ), and is of Scotch-Irish descent. Her parents are Charles Wesley and Letitia (Austin) Frazer; paternal grandparents:

John Ahair and Frances Amy (Jones) 

Frazer; maternal grandparents: Hugh R. and Eliza Ann (Ragan) Austin. She attended Higbee School and is a member of: Colonial Dames; D.A.R.; U.D.C.;

171 

Baptist Church; Democrat; American Red 

Cross; honorary award by the national council of the American Legion. She has been a writer of poetry and prose since she was eight years of age and published her first poem when she was fourteen; since then she has written for the leading magazines of America, including Harpers, Century, and Delineator. She is the author of such great poems as: "The 

Wizard of the Saddle," "The South's 

Gift to Fame," "Abraham Lincoln.''

She was named poet laureate of the U.C.V.A. of the entire south for life, (the first woman ever to hold the office in this organization). She was given two citations by the Italian Red Cross and a diploma, likewise two diplomas from two French academies. On April 22, 1884 she married Thomas R. Boyle, one of the leading attorneys of the city. Her father was a captain in the 5th Confederate infantry and while he was imprisoned the kindness shown by Pres. 

Lincoln to him caused her to take more interest in helping others than any other one thing, and therefore gaining her place in the world among the hearts of the people.

Goods Store in Binghamton, Tenn. which business he continued until March 1, 1917. In 1916-17 he was city tax assessor for the town of Binghamton. In 1918-19 he was Mayor of Binghamton. In 192122-23-24-25, he was a member of the

Shelby County Election Com. In 1926 he was elected member of Shelby County 

Election Primary Board serving for eight years, serving two years as chairman and four years as Secy. In 1928-29 he served as a member of the Shelby 

County Equalization Board. In 1929 he was Chairman of the same board. He served as a member of the Tenn. Legislature from Shelby County in 1929-31-33. 

On April 23, 1933 Mr. Hicks was appointed Shelby County Beer Com. serving until Sept. 1, 1936 at which time he was elected City tax assessor for the City of

Memphis which office he now holds. In 

1928 he was appointed as one of the five members of the Pension Board of the 

Memphis Fire and Police Dept., which post he now holds. In 1928 as Chairman of the Finance Committee of the Merton 

Ave. Baptist Church, he promoted the construction of the New Merton Ave. 

Baptist Church after wrecking the old one which was rebuilt with donations and free work, as a result of which the $95,000 structure was fully paid for; he was Sunday School Secy. of this church for a period of fourteen years; he was also a member of the Finance Committee for fourteen years and chairman of same committee for eight years.

HIGHSAW, JAMES LEONARD, Born at Pecan Gap, Texas on April 24, 1889; teacher; Scotch-Irish descent; married

Fredrick B. Highsaw and ( ); ma ternal grandparents: Jeremiah Shelton

Mason; Rotary, Memphis Chap., and Phi

Beta Kappa. In 1918 Prof. Highsaw founded the Memphis Technical High

School, the first institution of its kind in the State, an institution which is known throughout the entire State, having an enrollment of 1400 in its all-day session. 

From 1918 to 1932 Tech High had the largest night school in the South; at present, night sessions have been eliminated and transferred to other places. Prof. 

Highsaw began his teaching career in the public schools of Texas in 1904 in which profession he has been continuously engaged ever since. The Tech High School, as it is familiarly known all over the South, has now more than 7,000 alumni exerting a powerful influence over the life of Memphis. Prof. Highsaw was a 

Four-Minute man in Memphis during the 

World War. His great-grandfather,

James Ashley, was a member of the famous Ky. Buckskins Reg. and fought under Gen. Jackson at the battle of New 

Orleans. He is the father of two sons:

James Leonard, Jr., a graduate of Mem phis Technical High School, class of 

1931; of Princeton University, 1935, being Valedictorian of his class; he is now a student in Harvard Law School; and 

Robert Baker, graduate from Memphis

Tech High School in class of 1934 and now a senior at Princeton University. 

Prof. Highsaw's hobby is historical research. His wife, Mrs. Mattie May Highsaw, is a graduate of Oklahoma, Class of 1910, and was a very prominent teacher of the State at the time of her marriage. 

She is prominently identified with several civic organizations in Memphis.

JENNINGS, ALEXANDER EPSIA, 

Chairman, Executive Committee; born in 

Water Valley, Miss. on Sept. 10, 1866; 

Scotch-Irish descent; married Dixie Buford on Dec. 31, 1899; son of Capt. Zack

David and Charlotte Temple Hale Jen nings; paternal grandparents: Alexander 

S. and Helen Jackson Jennings; maternal grandparents: Shade and Amanda 

Maxwell Hale. Attended the public schools of Water Valley, Miss. and University of Miss., 1883-84; a member of the Baptist Church; Democrat; Mason; 

Shriner; Memphis Country Club; and a member of the Chamber of Commerce;

Chi Psi Fraternity. In his early life, beginning at age of twenty-one, he became engaged in the mercantile business which he continued for a period of a half century. In Nov. 1899 he became a member of the Baptist Church. During Christ mas, 1899, he began building the Baptist 

Orphanage at Jackson, Miss. In 1907 he and his family erected the Jennings Memorial Bldg. at Clinton, Miss. In 1908 he erected another Memorial Hall to his mother at Blue Mountain, Miss. In 1919, he and his family purchased the Blue 

Mountain College from Lowrey and

Berry giving same to the Baptists of 

Miss. On Jan. 1, 1913 he removed to

It is now the largest hospital in the South. During the World War, Mr. Jennings was acting Chairman of the American Red Cross, under whose leadership Memphis became the most generous supporter of any city of the same size in the U.S. Mr. Jennings is the father of three children: David Buford, Louise, and Mrs. Esther Wilkes, wife of

Capt. B. B. Wilkes of the U. S. Army. Mr. 

Jennings' father was a soldier for four years in the Confederate Army and for two years under Gen. N. B. Forrest. Mr. 

Jennings' hobby has been one of looking after the poor and unfortunate.

Godon, Ga.-training draftees for service abroad. In May, 1919 he was discharged from the army. He entered the practice of law upon his return to Memphis, being connected with D. W. DeHaven, now supreme court judge of Tenn., until Mr. 

DeHaven became Chancellor in 1925; served on the planning board and board of adjustment for the City of Memphis by appointment of Mayor Overton, 19291936; on Oct. 11, 1933, he was appointed

C.M. by Chancellor D. W. DeHaven and 

L. D. Bijack which position he now holds. 

No man in Shelby County has given more freely of his time and efforts for the benefit of the city of Memphis than he.

He was elected five times a director in the Memphis and Shelby County Bar 

Assn., serving 13 years-over 4 years more than any other person ever served; served 7 years as Sec., 1 year as second vice-pres., one year as first vice-pres., and was elected pres. of the bar after having assumed the duties of C.M. and retired from practice. He now lives with his mother who is 84 years old. He is the 8th child of 11 children-2 girls and 4 boys now living. He is a member of the American Legion 40-8; Memphis 

Shelby County Bar Assn., Bar Assn. of 

Tenn., American Bar Assn. and has served on committees of all of these; 

K.C.; Alpha Tau Omega. His hobby is political history and he is now collecting books on history of Memphis and Tenn.

FOSTER, J. LON, Chief of Police, 

Nashville, Tenn.; born at Nashville, Tenn. on Nov. 12, 1879; English; married Nellie Buchanan Roach, Sept. 15, 1905; son of Benjamin Franklin and 

Annie Creech Foster; father's occupation: farmer; paternal grandparents: 

David Foster and 

Wiliams Foster; He maternal grandparents: John Creech and

Manda Green Creech. Attended the public schools of Davidson County; a member of the Baptist Church; Democrat; 

Mason; Shriner; Scottish Rite; W.O.W.

Mr. Foster worked for the N.C.R.R. as special agent for 4 years; as patrolman until he was promoted to sergeant, then to detective, then to inspector; he was made Chief of Police in Dec. 1928. is known as an efficient and hard-working officer and is well liked by all the officers under him. Under his administration, the 

City of Nashville's murder and felony rate has been greatly reduced. Besides his work with the police force he takes an active interest in all civic affairs. He has one child, Anna Lucile Foster West. 

His hobby is horseback riding. As a detective, Mr. Foster made an outstanding and unexcelled record in locating and apprehending fugitives from justice from other states. He states that he has enjoyed every minute of his service with the police dept. and reached his goal when appointed the Chief of Police, his early ambition as a patrolman. When he was first Chief, the Dept. had one car and under his administration he has asked for and obtained the radio patrol system and a large fleet of automobiles to cope with crime.

HART, JUDGE CHESTER K., Born in Smith County, Tenn. on Jan. 26, 1883;

Judge of Criminal Court; Scotch-Irish- 

English; married Francis Paule on August 4, 1931; son of William Young Hart and Margarette Marley Hart; paternal grandparents: Captain H. W. and Laura Young Hart; maternal grandparents: 

Henry J. Harley and Mary McCoy Har ley. Attended the public schools of Nashville; Joseph W. Allen College, Carthage, Tenn.; Cumberland University, LL.B., 1910; a member of the Church of Christ; 

Democrat; Mason; Jr. Order of American Mechanics; Royal Arch. Judge Hart was elected a judge of the criminal court of Davidson County in 1922 and has been elected twice since. In 1936 Judge Hart discovered that there were many thousands of fraudulent registrations of voters both real and fictitious, he immediately charged the grand jury to investigate the matter, which investigation resulted in the conviction of several prominent citizens, several of whom were office holders. It was his courageous action in this matter that cleaned up elections in Davidson County which had long been known to be corrupt.

MCMILLIN, LUCILLE FOSTER, Born at Shreveport, Louisiana; United States

Civil Service Commissioner; English- 

Irish; widow; daughter of James Martin 

Foster and Ellen Long Foster; paternal grandparents: Flavel Foster and Mary 

Hollingsworth; maternal grandparents: 

Dr. William Long and Emily Boggs; a member of the D.A.R.; U.D.C.; State

Historical Assn. of Tenn.; Chevy Chase Branch of National League of American Pen Women; Federation of Women's Clubs; National League of Women Vot ers; Tenn. State Tuberculosis Assn.;

James K. Polk Assn. of Tenn. (past 

Pres.); Deer Park Garden Club of Nashville (past Pres.). Mrs. McMillin is of colonial heritage and southern parentage; her early education was with governesses and tutors, completed at Mary Baldwin 

Seminary, Staunton, Va., with finishing courses in New York and Europe. When very young she became the bride of Hon.

Benton McMillin, then serving his twentieth year in the House of Representatives in Washington. While in her early twenties she was the first lady of Tennessee upon the election of Benton McMillin as governor, she being the youngest to ever achieve this distinction. 

With the election of Woodrow Wilson as

President of the U.S., the former governor was appointed Minister to Peru, serving for seven years. Mrs. McMillin became Chatelaine of the American Legation there. She was later in Guatemala for two years as diplomatic representative. Her interesting career continued with her election as national

Democratic Committee woman from Tenn., being the first to be elected to this post; during her tenure of office as such she called together and presided over a conference of Democratic women of the southern states held in Atlanta. Prior to the 1924 National Convention she was appointed Regional Director of organiza tion of Democratic women of the Southern states by the Hon. Cordell Hull and 

Chairman of the U.S. Civil Service Com mission at Washington, in 1933 by Pres. 

Franklin D. Roosevelt, which post she now holds; these two offices are the highest ever held by a Tennessee woman.

Her career has been one of the most colorful of all women in Tennessee history. Though her entire life, since the completion of her education, has been one of continuous and laborious public service, she has found time to promote many civic and social organizations, holding membership in a score or more; and from her connections in many fields of endeavor, she has been many times signally honored-among many others, she had conferred upon her the degree of Doctor of Humane Letters by Lincoln Memorial University, Harrogate, Tenn., at which time she delivered the Baccalaureate Address, being the first woman to receive this invitation. As a public speaker she is much sought after; her unexcelled humor and broad knowledge of public affairs generally have placed her in a position reached by but few women as a platform entertainer and political campaigner. She has also made a serious study of dramatic reading and has filled many professional engagements, presenting plays of modern Spanish dramatists; she speaks Spanish and 

French fluently. She mentions among her direct ancestors, Col. Ellis Cooke, who fought in the War of American Independence as Com. of Eastern Battalion, Morris County, N. J. Militia; Edward 

Howell, who came with his family to 

Boston in 1639 and was Asst. Gov. from 

1647-1653 of Connecticut; Rev. John

Moore, who was leader of a colony which established the town of Southampton,

Long Island.

MOORE, FRANK BRADLEY, Chief of Nashville Fire Dept.; born at Nashville, Tenn. on Feb. 16, 1872; married 

Daisy Thomas on Jan. 19, 1913; son of 

William Moore and Amanda Prickett 

Moore. Attended the public schools of 

Nashville and Davidson County; graduated from Hume Fogg High School; 

Mason; Shriner; began his services with 

Nash. Fire Dept. in 1892 as a pipeman, continuing with the City in this Dept. continuously except for two years when he retired to his farm and mercantile business; when he returned, after two years, his promotions came regularly until he became Chief in March 1928, in which capacity he is now serving. Prior to the time that Mr. Moore became Chief the City lost heavily in fire but owing to his wise management and many reforms, more modern equipment, more strenuous drill power, and the adoption of more strict building inspection, the fire loss has been considerably reduced. 

Prior to March 12, 1919, the members of the fire Dept. were on duty 24 hours each day, at that time the double platoon system went into effect. During his tenure of service the entire department became fully motorized on April 2, 1920. 

On Feb. 1, 1916 the pension law became effective providing for the pension pay on disability or retired pay.

MOUSSON, THEODORE DEWEY, 

Born at Nashville, Tenn. on March 16, 1898; Managing Director of the Knicker bocker Theatre; French-Swiss-German; married Bernice Englert; son of Karl 

David Heinrich Mousson; paternal grand parents: Johan David Albrecht Mousson and Martaretha Fred Bassinger Mousson; 

maternal grandparents: Valentine Stein hauer and Louise Krech. Educated in public schools; Hume Fogg; Fall's Business College; a member of the First 

Lutheran Church; Mason; Democrat;

Shriner. Dewey Mousson is a descendant of Peter Mousson of the early sixteenth century-Peter Mousson was a shipbuilder and established the town of De 

M ax d'Azil France. Mr. Mousson be gan his business career at an early age. 

While attending public schools, his afterschool hours were devoted to a bread route which he operated for a few years for his father. At fourteen years of age he suggested that his father open a moving picture show. His father opened a suburban theatre and left the management to his son. Within a year Dewey was operating three suburban theatres in Nashville and within another year he was also operating a Film Exchange. 

Several years later he joined the Crescent

Amusement Company, operated by Tony Sudekum, and has been connected with that organization since he began with the old Rialto Theatre. Within a few months Dewey was given the manager ship of the Knickerbocker Theatre of the circuit. His hobbies are baseball and swimming and he takes a delight in any and all outdoor sports. He is the originator of Kiddie Clubs and takes a delight in bringing happiness to children. 

Dewey also originated the "Toy Matinees" for the orphans and day home children, and today more than ten thousand theatres throughout the country are using his idea in furnishing moving picture programs and toys for their entertainment. His ancestors were doctors and statesmen; and Pont-à-Mousson, a township in France, was named after his early ancestors.

SISK, LEONARD, Of Nashville, Ten nessee, was elected National Vice Commander of the American Legion for 193637 at the 18th Annual National Conven tion at Cleveland, Ohio, on September 

24, 1936. He is a veteran of five major engagements of the World War in France and Belgium. He served as a machine gunner with the famous 30th U.S. Division in the fighting along the Ypres sector and the Somme offensive, where he was gassed and wounded and where he won the Order of the Purple Heart. Mr. 

Sisk was born at Pulaski, Tennessee, on 

Aug. 17, 1889; son of George W. and 

Lorena May Sisk. He was educated in the Pulaski and Franklin High Schools and the Y.M.C.A. School of Law at Nash ville.

He also attended the technical schools of the General Electric and the 

Westinghouse companies. Following 

America's entry into the World War, Mr. 

Sisk, although only 18 years old, enlisted in the U.S. Regular Army on Aug. 18, 1917, and was assigned to Co. A, 114th

Machine Gun Battalion, 30th Division. 

He went overseas with this outfit and was promoted to a sergeant. He spent 11 months in France. He was a victim of mustard and phosgene gas and was wounded by shrapnel on Sept. 29, 1918, at

PROMINENT TENNESSEANS the Bellicourt-Hiddenburg Line battle. 

Mr. Sisk now holds an active commission as Captain in the Tennessee National 

Guard, commanding the 105th Ordnance Company, 30th Division. Returning to 

Nashville upon the conclusion of his military service, Mr. Sisk was employed by the Tennessee Electric Power Company as a manager of power sales, which position he has held since 1919. He joined 

Nashville Post No. 5 of The American 

Legion in 1924, served as Post Vice Commander, and later as the Post Commander, as well as a member of the Post 

Executive Committee. He was elected 

Department Vice Commander for 1933-34 and Department Commander for 1934-35.

During his term as Department Commander, the Department of Tennessee sponsored legislation creating the Tennessee Crippled Children's Commission, under whose direction, with state, county and federal funds, thousands of crippled children are being cared for. Mr. Sisk directed a Legion survey of the state which disclosed that there were more than 10,000 crippled children in need of correction. His administration also successfully sponsored an appropriation by the state for the education of war orphans. He was also instrumental in the compilation of the names of all of the veterans of Davidson County, totalling 9,000. In addition to numerous department committees, Mr. Sisk also served on the National Convention Legislative 

Committees at the Miami and St. Louis conventions, and on the National Defense Committee at the Cleveland convention. 

In his spare time, he edits the monthly publication of the department of Ten nessee, The Tennessee Legionnaire. 

Sisk is married. He is a past president of the American Business Club; a member of the Nashville Lions Club; the 

Chamber of Commerce; University Club; and Oriental Club. He is also a member of the board of directors of the Nashville 

Y.M.C.A. and of the board of directors of the Nashville Community Chest.

Mr. Henry has made a good record as sheriff and during his administration he has thrice defeated the efforts of a mob to take from him prisoners. There have been no lynchings during his administration. There has been very little crime during his tenure of office. He was elected in 1936 by the biggest majority ever given a sheriff of

Giles County in its entire history.

ELLIS, CHARLES K., Attorney and farmer. Born of English-Irish-Dutch parentage in Grainger County, Tenn., on 

August 3, 1878, he was educated in the public schools of Grainger; at Madison 

Academy at Rutledge, Tennessee; Joppa 

Academy, Joppa, Tennessee, 1902; Maryville College, Maryville, Tenn., 1905-6. 

Member of the Methodist Church; Democrat; Jr. R.O.U.A.M. His parents were

Prior F. and Cordelia Virginia Shirley 

Ellis; paternal grandparents were Louis 

Mayberry and Martha Jennings Ellis; maternal grandparents were Patrick

Allen Shirley and Tabitha Curl Shirley. 

He attended the John R. Neil College of Law, Knoxville, Tennessee where he received his B.A. in 1928, his M.A. in 

1935. Judge Ellis was appointed County 

Judge of Grainger County on June 21, 1937 by Governor Gordon Browning. 

He was elected to the same office in 1922 and re-elected in 1926, serving for the full eight-year term. He was chairman of the Grainger County School 

Board from 1912 to 1916. In his early life he was a teacher in the public and academic schools of Grainger County for a period of two years. Judge Ellis was admitted to the bar in 1929 and is licensed to practice in all the courts of the state. He has been engaged in the general practice of law at Rutledge since 

1929. His many years of training and varied experience make him one of the best qualified men in his county and his services to the people of his county have made him one of the most popular citizens. His father was a soldier in the 

Civil War, fighting on the side of the Confederacy for the full duration of the conflict and was wounded at Marietta, Ga.; his paternal grandfather was a member of the state legislature and was a sheriff of Grainger County for six years before the Civil War. His maternal grandfather was one of the county's first chairmen of the County Court, serving for a number of years. Judge Ellis is one of the leading farmers of his county, and is also one of the leading livestock men of his county, in which pursuit he has been engaged all his life. 

He was a merchant for about six years. He is a member of the Board of Directors of the 

Citizens Bank and Trust Company, which place he has held for a number of years; he is also a member of the Finance Committee. He was responsible for the or ganization of the Farmers Mutual Fire 

Insurance Company, organized in 1913; he has been one of the officials of the company since its organization and is now its secretary and treasurer, which position he has held since 1916. The success of this company is the delight of his business connections. He was married to Miss Bertha Joe Anna Shaver on January 14, 1916.

LINDSEY, ISAAC MITCHELL, City 

Recorder of Sevierville, Tennessee. Judge 

Lindsey was first elected City Recorder of Sevierville in May, 1916, to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of

Recorder R. B. Robertson. He was reelected in 1918 and each successive two years thereafter, having served continuously for the past twenty-three years.

Prior to his election to this office he was a member of the County Court for a period of twenty-four years, during which time he served as chairman of the court for seven years. His long tenure of office has given him an understanding of public affairs in his town and county which few men have ever possessed. He is one of the best qualified men in the county, and one of the most popular citizens. He was educated in the public schools of Cocke County, where he was born on Feb. 7, 1862. Later he went to

Holston Seminary, 1878; Union Prep 

School, 1881. Member of the Methodist 

Church; Republican; W.O.W. He began his career on the farm where he remained for several years after his marriage to 

Miss Martha Jane Lovebay on June 25, 1882. In his early life he was a teacher in the public schools of Cocke and Sevier counties. His parents were John Wesley

Lindsey and Sarah Jane Smith Lindsey. 

His paternal grandparents were William and Phoebe Jane Broyles Lindsey; maternal grandparents were Mitchell and 

Fannie Elizabeth Leatherwood Smith. 

Mr. Lindsey has been very active in all religious and civic and public affairs which he deemed for the betterment of his community. His great-grandfather

Lindsey was a soldier under Gen. Jackson in the battle of the Horseshoe Bend where the scalping of the Indians was the order of the day-many scalps were brought through Sevierville, the home of the subject. His hobby is the collection of books.

LL.B. degree in 1901. He is a Democrat, Mason, T.O.O.F., and W.O.W. He married Miss Susie E. Watson on October 8, 1901. Mr. Paine began his career as a farmer in Sevier County but soon moved to Sevierville, Tennessee where he began the practice of law in March, 1895 and he is still engaged in the practice of his profession there, having one of the largest law practices in his section of the state. His reputation as a criminal lawyer is unsurpassed, being one of the most noted in the state. He has served in many public capacities, among which are his services as Judge of the

County. Judge Paine has for many years been an outstanding figure, both in political and other public affairs. His father was a soldier for 32 years in the Civil War, fighting on the side of the Confederacy. He is the father of three children: Mrs. Myrtle Waters, Tom C. 

Paine, and Earl W., all of Sevierville, and three grandchildren: Mary Louise,

SUTTON, CHARLIE HENRY, Mr. 

Sutton was first elected sheriff of Hancock County in August, 1932, and reelected in August, 1934 and again in 

August, 1936. He is the first man ever to be elected sheriff of his county three times in succession, and at each election by an overwhelming majority. Prior to his election to the office of sheriff he was engaged in general farming and livestock raising, in which he is still engaged in addition to his official duties. His father, George Sutton, was sheriff of Hancock

County for a period of four years from 1904-8 and had the reputation of having made one of the best officers the county had ever had; the popularity of Sheriff

Sutton is now attested by the overwhelming vote he has three times received. He was born in Hancock County on March

Nancy Dodson Sutton; his maternal grandparents were Henry and Martha

Culbertson Mahan. Educated in the public schools of Hancock County. Member of Baptist Church; Republican. Married 

Miss Nora Markum on May 24, 1925. 

Father of eight children: Lizzie, Mary 

Lee, Joe Mitchell, George, Bernice, Hence, Hugh James, and Evelyn Ruth.

SCOTT, HENRY EUGENE, President of Burritt College, Spencer, Tennessee.

Mr. Scott was born at McMinnville, Tennessee on Dec. 18, 1890, of Scotch descent. 

His parents were Levi and Nannie Lockhart Scott; his father was a farmer and public official; his mother came from 

Grundy County. His paternal grandparents were John and Mary Martin 

Scott; maternal grandparents were Holman and Nancy Hunter Lockhart; educated in the public schools and Irving 

College, Warren County; graduated at

Burritt College and University of Tennessee. Member of Church of Christ; 

Mason; Odd Fellow; Democrat; M.W.A.

Married Miss Notie Lewis Dec. 31, 1914. 

Mr. Scott was elected President of Burritt College in 1918, which position he now holds. Prior to becoming president, he was a teacher of Mathematics at Burritt College for a period of three years; he has served as County Superintendent of Van Buren County for a period of twelve years, ten of which was during his term as president of the above-mentioned institution. He has served as Chairman of the Red Cross of Van Buren County since 1918. He has served on the various committees handling the activities of government work in Van Buren County during the administration of F. D. Roosevelt.

His grandfather Scott was a soldier in the Civil War, for its entire duration, participating in some of the most important engagements fought in Tennessee. Mr. Scott, during his term of office as President of Burritt College, has assisted a large number of boys and girls who were not able to finance their education. He is the father of three children: 

Henry Eugene Scott, Jr., 21; Mary 

Frances Scott, 16; and Gwendolyn Lewis 

Scott, 11. His hobby is sports.

MITCHELL, ROBERT H., Landowner, and foreman of Coffee County Grand 

Jury. Born in Bedford County on Oct. 

10, 1845, of Scotch-Irish ancestry, his parents were Tarlton and Peggy Brinkly 

Mitchell; his father was a farmer and was born at Creedmore, N. C. His paternal grandparents were John and Sallie 

Johnson Mitchell of Maryland; maternal grandparents were Bob and Betsy Low 

Brinkley of N. C. Educated in the public schools of Bedford County, Tennessee. Member of the Lutheran Church. 

Mr. Mitchell is one of Middle Tennessee's pioneer citizens and, notwithstanding the fact that he is 92 years of age, is still very active looking after his farming interests which are very large. He is one of the largest landowners in Tennessee. 

He has been for many years and still is foreman of the Coffee County Grand Jury. 

His forefathers were among those who helped to settle Tennessee. He has several sons, all of whom have made wonderful successes. He is the father of eight children, all of whom are living. His wife was Minerva Carroll before their marriage in 1870. Mr. Mitchell started out in life as a poor boy and by hard work and thrift is today a very wealthy man. 

OWENS, MRS. CORNELIA, Manufac turer. Born in Moore County, Tennessee on Sept. 2, 1887, of Welch-English descent, to James F. and Bettie Copeland 

Spencer. Mrs. Owens was formerly Miss

Cornelia Spencer of Moore County. 

Shortly after her marriage to Claude 

Owens on January 8, 1904, she moved, together with her husband, to Tullahoma, Tennessee, where she has lived ever since.

She is the pioneer manufacturer in the 

United States of Candlewick bedspreads, and her business has grown from a small beginning to a quarter of a million dollar business. She is one of the state's outstanding business women. Her bedspreads are sold all over the world. She is a pioneer like her forefathers. Her paternal grandparents were William and ( ) Frame Spencer; maternal grandparents were Nicholas and Rhoda Eslick

Copeland. Educated in the public schools of Moore County, Tennessee. Member of the Primitive Baptist Church. She is the mother of six sons; Roy, Wilfred, Virgil, James, Charles, and Billie; she has two grandsons, Robert Spencer, and Dale

Richard. 

RICHARDSON, THOMAS EDWARD, Postmaster at Tullahoma, Tennessee. Mr. 

Richardson was appointed Postmaster by

President Calvin Coolidge on Feb. 5, 1924, and was re-appointed twice by President 

Hoover, serving in this capacity until 

April, 15, 1937. He has been an efficient and trustworthy postmaster, giving the best of mail service to his patrons during his tenure of office. Prior to his appointment as Postmaster, he was a retail merchant in the town of Tullahoma. He takes an active interest in all civic affairs and is one of Tullahoma's outstanding and leading citizens. He is a former alderman of the town of Tullahoma and is at the present time a member of the 

Coffee County Court. Born in Coffee 

County, Tennessee on October 30, 1885, of Scotch parentage. His parents were

Robert Harris Richardson and Delilah D. 

Yell Richardson. Paternal grandparents were Thomas Edward and ( ) Richardson. Maternal grandparents were

Marion and ( ) Short Yell. Edu cated in the public schools of Coffee 

County, Tennessee. Member of the K.P., Jr. Order; Secretary, Rotary Club; Past 

President of the Rotary Club; Republican.

Married Isla Paschal on June 15, 1911. 

He is the father of one child, Mrs. Thurel

J. Poe of Tullahoma. His hobby is civic affairs.

11, 1906, of English-Irish ancestry, to

Charles H. and Dora Tony Davis. Pa ternal grandparents were Reuben and

Lucinda Summers Davis; maternal grand parents were John and Julia Scott Tony.

Educated in the public and high schools of Morgan County, at Wartburg. Mem ber of the Baptist Church; a Democrat.

Mrs. Adkins was appointed Postmaster at Wartburg on October 1, 1933 by Pres.

U. S. postal service, Mrs. Adkins has proven her ability to be a postmaster and the condition of the affairs of her office prove her efficiency. Her maternal grandmother, Julia Scott, was a descendant of the Scott family which was among the earliest settlers of this section of the state. Mrs. Adkins married D. N. Adkins on December 3, 1922. She is the mother of four children: Juanita, 13; Donald, 12; Virginia Lee, 11; Betty Lou, 9.
